newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets Arafat to try to boost Mideast role.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets Arafat to try to boost Mideast role.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin welcomed Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to the Kremlin on Tuesday, hoping to boost Moscow's profile in Middle East peace talks so far dominated by Washington.

The meeting was the latest in a diplomatic flurry for Yeltsin, laid low by heart problems for much of last year. But it appeared to be more an exercise in mutual back-slapping than a forum for any new initiatives.

"I am very glad to see you in good health," Arafat told Yeltsin through an interpreter, kissing the Kremlin leader three times each on the cheeks and forehead. "It is a great joy for the whole world," he said.

Yeltsin, looking lively but with a return of some of the puffiness around his face which has appeared on-and-off during months of illness, greeted Arafat with a broad smile. "Hello my good friend," he said.
A Kremlin statement issued after the talks played on the traditional good relations between Moscow and the Palestinians and took a robust line, but avoided specifics.

"It was firmly stated that Russia, as a co-sponsor of the Middle East peace process, will continue energetic efforts with the aim of cooperating in the resolution of problems, the establishment of peace and good-neighbourly relations," it said.

"The president is impressed by the constructive course of the Palestinian leadership headed by Y. Arafat," said the statement, adding that Arafat had noted Russia's "weighty contribution" to the peace process.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky later told a news briefing that Yeltsin had accepted an invitation by Arafat to attend celebrations in Bethlehem in the year 2000 to mark the aniversary of Christianity, and that Yeltsin had accepted.
Russia has been a joint sponsor, with the United States, of the Middle East peace process and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is expected in Moscow in March.

But Moscow's influence in the region has declined since Soviet days, although Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said that Russia had never left the Middle East. "I think that simply it was less noticeably active on the scene," he said.

Netanyahu met President Bill Clinton and other U.S. officials in Washington last week to discuss ways to keep the Middle East peace momentum going after Israel's withdrawal of troops from Hebron in the West Bank.
Russia had little to do with the U.S.-brokered peace deal last month under which Israel agreed to hand over 80 percent of the town of Hebron to the Palestine Liberation Organisation.

"After giving no help in settling this aspect of the problem (Hebron), Russian diplomacy is trying to show itself in the next stage of the peace process," the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper commented this week.

On Friday Yeltsin will meet U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to try to overcome a bitter row over NATO plans to expand into eastern Europe and prepare for a summit with President Bill Clinton in Helsinki next month.
The meetings give Yeltsin, 66, the opportunity to flex his muscles on the world stage after pneumonia and heart surgery, although Russia has found itself cornered in the NATO row.
Russian officials have recognised that there is nothing they can do to stop NATO expansion, but are hoping to persuade the alliance to make concessions to appease its security concerns.
Yastrzhemsky said recent spats between Russia and the U.S. over arms sales might also come up in the talks with Albright, accusing the U.S. of using "inadmissible" tactics.

"When they lose the tough competitive battle to Russia some of our partners, in the given case the United States, often start using all admissible and inadmissible means, often behind the scenes, to discredit Russian arms," he said.
He cited contracts for the sale of anti-aircraft missiles to Cyprus and Mi-17 helicopters to Colombia, both of which he said would soon be honoured despite U.S. objections.
